realism_constraints: No modern forensic DNA analysis or electronic surveillance
Limited police procedural methods relying on observation and deduction
Travel and communication constrained to horse-drawn vehicles, telegrams, and boats
location: London and environs, including Upper Norwood and the Thames river
institution: Scotland Yard and unofficial consulting detective Sherlock Holmes
crime_subtype: poisoned dart murder with secret access

cast.name: Dr. John Watson
cast.stakes: assist Holmes and protect Miss Morstan

cast.name: Miss Mary Morstan
cast.motive_seed: inheritance and justice for her father

cast.name: Jonathan Small
opportunity_channels: secret access via roof and accomplice

surface_summary: Bartholomew Sholto is found dead in a locked room with no apparent means of entry or exit for the murderer. A valuable treasure has been stolen, and suspicion falls on his brother Thaddeus and household staff. The presence of a wooden-legged man and mysterious small footprints complicate the case.
accepted_facts: Bartholomew Sholto was found dead with a poisoned thorn in his scalp
The door and window of the room were locked from the inside
A secret trap-door in the roof allowed access to the room
A valuable treasure was stolen from the house
inferred_conclusions: Thaddeus Sholto murdered his brother to claim the treasure
The murder was committed through the locked door or window
The wooden-legged man acted alone in the crime
mechanism_description: The murderer entered the victim's room by climbing up the roof and descending through a secret trap-door. The accomplice Tonga, a small Andaman Islander, climbed down a rope lowered by Jonathan Small and used poisoned darts to kill Bartholomew. They then lowered the treasure chest through the trap-door and escaped the same way.
delivery_path: Jonathan Small and Tonga approach the house at night
Jonathan climbs to the roof and lowers a rope
Tonga climbs down the rope into the victim's room
Tonga uses a poisoned dart to kill Bartholomew Sholto
They lower the treasure chest through the trap-door
Tonga climbs back up the rope and the trap-door is secured
outcome_result: Jonathan Small and Tonga are captured after a chase on the Thames, and the treasure is recovered but found to be missing its contents.

false_assumption.statement: The murderer must have entered through the locked door or window.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The door and window were locked from the inside, so it is logical to assume the killer used one of these points. No other entry points were initially visible.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It hides the existence of a secret trap-door in the roof that provided access, and the involvement of an accomplice who climbed down a rope.

supporting_points: He was the last person seen with Bartholomew
He had a motive related to the treasure
He was found in a disturbed state near the crime scene
He had access to the house and the victim
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was locked out of the victim's room at the time of death and had an alibi

red_herrings.description: Thaddeus Sholto's nervousness and quarrel with his brother suggest guilt.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was anxious about the treasure and family disputes but was not the murderer.

red_herrings.description: The butler Lal Rao is suspected of complicity due to his presence and character.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was merely a loyal servant and had no involvement in the murder or theft.

closed_circle.rationale: All suspects had access to the house, but only Jonathan Small and Tonga had the means and motive to commit the murder and theft, while others were cleared by alibis or lack of evidence.

time_anchors: Bartholomew locked himself in at 10 PM
Thaddeus left the room after 10 PM
Launch Aurora left at about 3 AM
time_windows: Murder occurred between 10 PM and discovery
Escape by launch shortly after murder
trust_channels: Communication between Jonathan Small and Tonga

inference_path.observation: The door and window of the victim's room were locked from the inside
inference_path.correction: There is a secret trap-door in the roof providing access
inference_path.effect: The murderer did not enter through conventional means
required_evidence: Inspection of the locked room and trap-door by Holmes
Witness statement from housekeeper Mrs. Bernstone about locked door

inference_path.observation: Footprints of a wooden stump and small naked feet found in the room
inference_path.correction: Two perpetrators: one with a wooden leg and a small accomplice
inference_path.effect: Identifies two distinct criminals with different physical characteristics
required_evidence: Footprint impressions in creosote and dust
Description of Tonga's small stature and wooden leg of Jonathan Small

inference_path.observation: Poisoned thorn found in victim's scalp
inference_path.correction: Murder was committed using a poisoned dart from a blow-pipe
inference_path.effect: Cause of death is poisoning, not blunt force trauma

inference_path.observation: Rope found in the victim's room leading to the roof
inference_path.correction: Murderer climbed down the rope from the roof
inference_path.effect: Confirms secret access route and method of entry/exit

inference_path.observation: Toby the dog tracked scent from creosote on the rope
inference_path.correction: The accomplice dipped foot in creosote to climb down
inference_path.effect: Identifies the accomplice's route and presence
required_evidence: Creosote stains on rope and footprints

inference_path.observation: Launch Aurora was missing and later found at Jacobson's Yard
inference_path.correction: Launch was used for escape and hidden at a boatyard
required_evidence: Witness statement from Mrs. Smith about launch departure

inference_path.observation: Jonathan Small and Tonga captured after chase on Thames
inference_path.correction: They are the culprits responsible for murder and theft
inference_path.effect: Case solved with arrest of guilty parties
required_evidence: Eyewitness accounts of chase and capture
Physical evidence linking them to crime scene

discriminating_test.design: Holmes uses the presence of creosote on the rope and footprints to prove the accomplice climbed down from the roof, which is inaccessible by other means. He also uses Toby the dog to track the scent trail leading to the escape launch, confirming the route and method of escape.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test reveals the secret access route via the roof trap-door and the involvement of two criminals with distinct physical traits. It disproves entry through locked doors or windows.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: Finding creosote footprints and rope marks consistent with climbing and tracking the scent trail to the launch confirms the mechanism of the crime.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all necessary clues including the locked room, the secret trap-door, the footprints of a wooden leg and small feet, the poisoned thorn, and the rope. Holmes's reasoning is based on observable physical evidence and logical deduction. The presence of the creosote and the dog's tracking provide concrete leads that the reader could follow. The false assumptions and red herrings are clearly presented and can be questioned by attentive readers.
